英文.全文:
JNR 24 series passenger cars

The JNR 24 series was a passenger car designed and manufactured by Japanese National Railways (JNR). Although the early Type 24 and Type 25 differed in their class B sleeper equipment, they were treated as a single series with a common basic structure designed and built using the centralized power supply system, and are therefore described together in this article.

== Overview ==
Construction began in 1973 (Showa 48) as rolling stock for sleeper limited express trains (the so-called "Blue Trains"), replacing the 14 series, and continued until 1980 (Showa 55) with the aim of replacing the aging 20 series and improving passenger service facilities. While it was well received by users for its service facilities, an improvement over the 20 series, some also lamented that it offered no entirely new services to surprise passengers.
The exterior, equipment, bogies, CL automatic brakes, and other specifications were largely based on the 14 series (sleeper cars), but thorough fire prevention measures were applied, and, like the earlier 20 series, a "centralized power supply system" was adopted in which service power was supplied from an independent power car to the passenger cars. Accordingly, taking into consideration the current capacity of the entire train formation, a feedthrough for a three-phase alternating current auxiliary circuit for power supply was provided on both the ocean side and the mountain side of the formation.
For this reason, they could not be coupled with distributed-power cars such as the 14 and 12 series, but in later years, by drawing through only broadcast jumper cables while keeping the power systems self-contained within each series, combined operation became possible, and mixed coupling was seen on trains such as the express "Hamanasu" and the "Sakura", "Hayabusa", "Akatsuki", and "Naha".

=== Development background ===
In 1971 (Showa 46), JNR developed and expanded its fleet of the 14 series passenger cars, which adopted a "distributed power system" supplying service power for passenger cars from diesel engine-driven generators under the floor. However, the Hokuriku Tunnel fire accident of 1972 (Showa 47) raised concerns that placing diesel engines, a potential source of fire, beneath passenger compartments posed problems from the standpoint of fire safety. Production of the 14 series Type 14 was halted, and this type was developed as its replacement.

== Vehicle description ==
This section describes the specifications at the time of completion (as built).

=== 24 series ===
This was the name given to the initial type manufactured in 1973 (Showa 48). The class A sleepers, class B sleepers, and dining cars largely followed the design of the 14 series, but differed externally in that the attendants' handrails were moved toward the center of the car body side, except at the doors, and shortened. Interior equipment and air conditioning units (Type AU76, 15,000 kcal/h × 2) were essentially equivalent to the 14 series, but flame-retardant measures were thoroughly applied, such as changing the sleeper frames from FRP to aluminum. Since production shifted to the 24 series Type 25 the following year, 1974, orders for this group were placed only once, and production was limited to 118 cars.
In addition, to distinguish them from the newly introduced Type 25, they came to be called "24 series Type 24" for convenience (a retronym). However, due to this history, even when the term "24 series" is used alone afterwards, it sometimes refers only to the Type 24 covered in this section.
The class A sleepers were open-plan Pullman type, the same as the 14 series class A sleepers. The class B sleepers were initially three-tier berths, but between December 1982 (Showa 57) and July 1983 (Showa 58) all cars were rebuilt to the same two-tier arrangement as the Type 25, by removing the upper berths and fixing the middle berths in the raised position to serve as the new upper berths.
They were initially allocated to the Mukainomachi Depot of the Osaka Railway Bureau (later Kyoto General Depot, now the Kyoto Branch of Suita General Rolling Stock Center) and used on the "Akatsuki" and "Suisei". In the March 1975 (Showa 50) timetable revision, all but a few cars were transferred to the Shinagawa Passenger Car District of the Minami-Tokyo Railway Bureau (later Shinagawa Depot, now the Tamachi Center of Tokyo General Rolling Stock Center) and used on the "Hayabusa", "Fuji", and "Izumo"; in the October 1976 (Showa 51) timetable revision they were transferred again to the Aomori Depot of the Morioka Railway Bureau (later Aomori Rolling Stock Center, now the Aomori branch office of Morioka Rolling Stock Center) and used on the "Yuzuru" and "Nihonkai". Furthermore, in the October 1980 (Showa 55) timetable revision, some Aomori-based cars were transferred to the Akita Operating District of the Akita Railway Bureau (now the Minami-Akita Center of Akita General Rolling Stock Center) and replaced the "Akebono", the last sleeper express to use the 20 series. Then, in the November 1982 (Showa 57) timetable revision, all cars remaining at Aomori were transferred to Akita and were also used on the "Dewa", newly established by upgrading an express train, in addition to the "Yuzuru" and "Akebono".

=== 24 series Type 25 ===
A minor-change variant of the 24 series (Type 24), manufactured from the second half of fiscal 1973 (fiscal Showa 48). At the time of manufacture, anticipating the imminent extension opening of the Sanyo Shinkansen between Okayama and Hakata, and the decline in sleeper express passengers due to the development of air transportation networks, the class B sleeper cars were redesigned from the conventional three-tier berths to two-tier berths in order to reduce capacity and improve habitability. They were first introduced on part of the "Akatsuki" and "Suisei" in April 1974 (Showa 49).
Moreover, to minimize as far as possible the reduction in capacity caused by the two-tier berths, a stopgap measure was taken: the toilets were arranged in a single bay longitudinally, the dressing room was eliminated to secure space for one row (two passengers), and, comparing the OhaNe 24 and OhaNe 25, a 17-row layout was achieved, one row more per car. Externally, while the Type 24 had white bands (Cream No. 10), the Type 25 had stainless steel bands from the beginning of manufacture, from the standpoint of saving labor in the painting process. Minor changes were made several times depending on the production period, resulting in detailed variations such as car body shape. Also, since capacity was reduced, the capacity of the air conditioning units was slightly lowered (Type AU77, 10,000 kcal/h × 2), and since there was surplus headroom in the interior, the air conditioning ducts were moved from the corridor side to the center. For fire prevention, smoke detectors were installed in the corridors of the OhaNe 25, near ventilation openings, and near the toilets. The OROne 25 had heat detectors installed on the ceilings of its private rooms.
The name "24 series Type 25" was a convenient designation to distinguish the two-tier open class B sleeper cars OhaNe 25 and OhaNefu 25 from the conventional three-tier 24 series; even after the appearance of the 24 series Type 25, cars with type number 24 such as the Kani 24, Sushi 24, and Oha 24 appeared. Naturally, there was no difference between the two in basic systems such as brakes and service power. The 24 series Type 25 received the 15th Laurel Prize from the Japan Railfan Club in 1975 (Showa 50).

== Newly built cars ==

=== Class A sleeper ===

==== OROne 24 ====

0 subseries
An open-room two-tier (Pullman style) class A sleeper. The body structure follows that of the OROne 14, with a smoking room and dressing room at the car ends. After their initial allocation, all nine cars were transferred in step with the changes in trains using the 24 series Type 24, from Mukainomachi to Shinagawa, Aomori, and Akita; however, when the "Ginga" was converted to 24 series operation in the final years of JNR, one car (No. 6) was transferred to the Miyahara Passenger Car District; eight cars were inherited by East Japan Railway Company (JR East), and one by West Japan Railway Company (JR West). All JR East cars were transferred to Aomori in 1988 (Showa 63); in 1991 (Heisei 3) one car was rebuilt as a SuroNe 24 550 subseries, and scrapping began in 1997 (Heisei 9). The three cars that remained until the end were scrapped as follows: No. 2 on September 8, 2012 (Heisei 24), No. 4 on March 4, 2013 (Heisei 25), and No. 5 on March 19, 2013 (Heisei 25).

==== OROne 25 ====

0 subseries
A private-room sleeper manufactured in 1976 (Showa 51) for use on trains between Tokyo and Kyushu and the San'in region. It has 14 single-person private rooms, each equipped with a table that doubles as a washstand. On cars 11 and 12, the structure of the lower part of the table/washstand was improved so that the feet of a seated person could fit under the window-side washstand. Three cars (8, 11, 12) were rebuilt as the 700 subseries in the final years of JNR; of the remainder, three were inherited by JR East and six by Kyushu Railway Company (JR Kyushu). The six JR Kyushu cars were used on the "Hayabusa" and "Fuji", but No. 3 was scrapped on September 9, 1996 (Heisei 8), and the remaining five cars were rebuilt into the 14 series in 2005 (Heisei 17) as the OROne 15 3000 subseries (since only 3000 was added to the original numbers, 3003 is a missing number). Following the appearance of other private sleepers, it was given the nickname "Single Deluxe" in 1986 (Showa 61). The last car to remain, No. 7, was scrapped on March 1, 2021 (Reiwa 3).

=== Three-tier class B sleeper ===

==== OhaNe 24 ====
A three-tier class B sleeper belonging to the basic 24 series form.

0 subseries (1–67)
A newly built class B sleeper manufactured in 1973 (Showa 48). Capacity was 48 when new and 32 after conversion to two-tier berths. The body follows the OhaNe 14. As of April 2015 (Heisei 27), five cars were based at Aomori, but all were scrapped by November of that year.

==== OhaNefu 24 ====
A three-tier class B sleeper and brake van belonging to the basic 24 series form.

0 subseries (1–27)
Manufactured in 1973. Capacity was 45 when new and 30 after conversion to two-tier berths. The body shape is a structure based on the SuhaNefu 14. Cars 16–18 were transferred to the 14 series in 1977 (Showa 52), with a power engine and generator installed under the floor, becoming SuhaNefu 14 101–103. As of April 2015 (Heisei 27), ten cars were based at Aomori, but all were scrapped by November of that year.

=== Two-tier class B sleeper ===

==== OhaNe 25 ====
A two-tier class B sleeper belonging to the 24 series Type 25.

0 subseries (1–91)
A class B sleeper newly built with the berths of the OhaNe 24 changed to two-tier. Like the OhaNe 24, the upper berths are equipped with a button-operated automatic lifting device. As of April 2015 (Heisei 27), two cars were based at Sapporo, but all were scrapped in March 2016 (Heisei 28).

100 subseries (101–246)
Cars in which the upper berths were fixed to save labor. As a result, the height of the windows on the berth side is smaller than that of the 0 subseries. As of April 1, 2016 (Heisei 28), three cars were based at Oku, but all were scrapped by May of that year.

==== OhaNefu 25 ====
A two-tier class B sleeper and brake van belonging to the 24 series Type 25.

0 subseries (1–47)
Manufactured between 1974 and 1976. The end on the conductor's room side is finished with a rounded roof and half-gable (clipped gable), following the SuhaNefu 14, the 14 series sleeper. A tail light was also installed on the washroom-side coupling face. As an external feature, on cars 1–27 the jumper coupler mounting on the conductor's room side is at a high position near the tail light, while on cars 28 onward it is at a low, waist-level position from the time of completion (the photo shows a car from No. 28 onward). Although cars 1–27 were later relocated to the waist-level position, a square protrusion remains at the original position on the exterior.
As a replacement for No. 18, which was scrapped due to an accident in 1976 (Showa 51), No. 47 of the 0 subseries was additionally manufactured for replenishment, even though production of the 100 subseries had already begun at that time.

100 subseries (101–157)
Manufactured between 1976 and 1977. The upper berths were fixed, and with this the height of the windows on the berth side was also reduced. Externally, the end on the conductor's room side was changed to a full gable.
This subseries was designed with the jumper coupler as a "one-sided" type, with the intent that the conductor's room and the power car always face in opposite directions within a single train formation; as a result, it became impossible to freely change the direction of cars when coupling and operating them during formation.
As of April 2015 (Heisei 27), two cars were based at Aomori, but all were scrapped in November of that year.

200 subseries (201–221)
Manufactured between 1978 (Showa 53) and 1980 (Showa 55). Since the aforementioned 100 subseries (full gable) presented obstructions during coupling and uncoupling work, this was reflected in improved workability: the end on the conductor's room side was made a half-gable (also called a half-clipped gable; the gable design with a gentle receding angle), and the jumper coupler was returned to the same direction-changeable structure as the 0 subseries. The structure of the other parts of the body is almost the same as the 100 subseries.
In 1991 (Heisei 3), cars 218 and 220 were transferred to the 14 series with a power engine and generator installed under the floor, becoming SuhaNefu 14 551 and 552. As of April 2015 (Heisei 27), five cars were based at Sapporo, Aomori, and Oku, but all were scrapped by November of that year.

=== Dining car ===

==== Oshi 24 ====

0 subseries (1–5)
A dining car manufactured at the same time as the basic 24 series form. The basic structure follows the Oshi 14, but in finer details, further fire prevention measures were taken, such as changing the interior display shelves and the hinged doors at the dining room entrance to aluminum. Later, when the 24 series Type 25 was introduced on Blue Trains serving Tokyo Station, the production of new dining cars for that group was curtailed and this type was diverted from the Type 24 group; it was therefore used with its white bands unchanged and could be easily identified within a formation. From 1985 (Showa 60), the band color was progressively changed to silver (silver tape like that of the lounge cars, not a stainless band). Subsequently, in 1985 (Showa 60), in the final years of JNR, all cars were rebuilt as the 700 subseries and the type ceased to exist.

=== Power supply cars ===
The 14 series, built as the successor to the 20 series, had adopted the distributed power system, but concerns about safety were raised due to the Hokuriku Tunnel fire accident, so this series reverted to the centralized power system using power supply cars.
At the time of their appearance, the separation of passenger and freight services was progressing, and because the first cars built had no passenger space at all, the "Ya" of works cars (business-use cars) was used. Later, they came to be used for newspaper transportation, and because a baggage room was provided, the "Ni" of baggage cars came to be used.
From the early 1990s, on limited express trains using 24 series passenger cars that served Ueno Station, such as the "Hokutosei", "Dewa", and "Akebono", the power supply cars were coupled at the rear end facing Ueno as a noise countermeasure at Ueno Station.

==== Maya 24 → Kaya 24 ====
A type that appeared in 1973 (Showa 48). Ten cars (1–10) were manufactured by Nippon Sharyo, Fuji Heavy Industries, and Niigata Tekko, and were initially completed as the Maya 24. The engine room was equipped with two power generation units combining intercooler turbo diesel engines of Type DMF31Z-G (430 PS / 1,200 rpm) with Type DM95 generators (300 kVA), enabling three-phase alternating current power of 60 Hz / 440 V to be supplied to all cars. The bogies are the coil-spring Type TR54C. In addition, because the power generation equipment of this series was under fully automatic control, making unattended operation of the power cars possible, the technician's room and technician's toilet installed on 20 series power cars were abolished in this series.
At completion, all cars were allocated to the Mukainomachi Depot and used on sleeper expresses between Kansai and Kyushu. However, in 1974 (Showa 49), because a baggage loading space with a load of 0.5 t was installed in the business room at Takasago Works for newspaper transport, the tare weight changed, and all cars were redesignated as the Kaya 24. After the later-described Kani 24 was introduced, two cars were transferred to the Shinagawa Passenger Car District together with the 24 series sleepers in 1975 (Showa 50) and, due to baggage loading capacity, used on the "Izumo"; when the Type 25 was introduced at the Shinagawa Passenger Car District, they were transferred to the Aomori Depot together. The remainder were also transferred to Aomori in 1980 (Showa 55) together with the Type 25 class B sleepers (for a time two cars were based at Akita) and used on the "Nihonkai", "Yuzuru", "Akebono", "Dewa", and "Chokai". Subsequently, three cars were transferred to the Miyahara Passenger Car District and also used on the "Nihonkai", "Tsurugi", and "Ginga". When transferred to Aomori and Akita, they were equipped for pushing transfer operation between the Oku Passenger Car District (now Oku Rolling Stock Center), their overnight base, and Ueno Station (with a brake pipe connection in the conductor's room and the installation of manual windshield wipers).
In the final years, engine replacement renewals like those of the Kani 24 were not carried out; the Aomori-based cars were used on the "Hakutsuru", "Akebono", and "Nihonkai", and the Miyahara-based cars on the "Ginga" and "Nihonkai"; all cars were scrapped in 2003 (Heisei 15) and the type ceased to exist.

==== Kani 24, 0 subseries ====
With the conversion of the "Akatsuki" and "Suisei" to the 24 series Type 25, 25 cars were manufactured by Nippon Sharyo, Fuji Heavy Industries, and Niigata Tekko between 1974 (Showa 49) and 1976 (Showa 51). Cars 1–8 had micro-skirts, but these were later removed. The generators in the engine room were the same as those of the Maya 24, but a baggage room with a load of 3 t was installed, and the car body length was 18.5 m, 1.5 m longer than that type. Because they belong to the Type 25, the decorative bands were changed to stainless steel. Note that No. 6 is an anomalous car whose stainless band beside the headmark was installed at the bottom edge. The rear end face was non-through-type, like the Maya. However, on the second-batch cars 9–25, the micro-skirt at the bottom edge of the end face was omitted. The bogies are Type TR66B.
In the JNR era they were allocated to Shinagawa, Mukainomachi, and Miyahara and used on sleeper expresses to Tokyo, Kansai–Kyushu, and on the Nihonkai (Sea of Japan) trunk line. Subsequently, cars transferred to Aomori and Akita (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 19, 20, 21) were equipped for pushing transfer operation between the Oku Passenger Car District (now Oku Rolling Stock Center), the base on the up side, and Ueno Station (with a brake pipe connection in the conductor's room and the installation of manual windshield wipers).
Between 1987 (Showa 62) and 1988 (Showa 63), nine cars were rebuilt into the severe cold weather 500 subseries (for the Hokutosei) at Tsuchizaki Works (now Akita General Rolling Stock Center). Cars equipped for pushing transfer operation were preferentially assigned to these.
At JR East, some cars underwent body renewal modification work, including replacement of the diesel engine with Type DMF15Z-G and the generator with Type DM109, noise countermeasures, and car body refurbishment. Some cars formerly based at JR Kyushu showed cases such as omission of the white frame around the train name indicator and lowering of the lower of the end-face decorative bands to the bottom edge.
As of April 2016 (Heisei 28), four cars (10, 12–14) used on the "Twilight Express" were in service, allocated to Miyahara, but all were scrapped by July of that year. Of these, No. 13 was initially green with the silver band unchanged. The JR mark in Twilight livery colors is affixed beside the conductor's room door, but on No. 14 alone it is affixed beside the baggage room door, like the blue cars.

==== Kani 24, 100 subseries ====
A group added with the conversion of the "Asakaze", "Seto", and "Aki" to the 24 series Type 25; 16 cars (101–116) were manufactured by Niigata Tekko and Fuji Heavy Industries in 1977 (Showa 52) and 1980 (Showa 55). The basic structure is the same as the 0 subseries, but because the baggage room load was changed to 5 t following increased baggage handling for trains serving Tokyo, the car body length was extended by 1 m to 19.5 m. The rear end face was also changed from non-through-type to a gable-type through type, and the baggage room roof section was also changed to a normal roof. It also became possible to supply power from both sides of the car. The bogies were changed to Type TR66C.
In the JNR era they were allocated to Shinagawa, Mukainomachi, and Shimonoseki and used on sleeper expresses to Tokyo and Kansai–Kyushu. In particular, the "Asakaze" Nos. 1 and 4, handled by Shinagawa, were in principle assigned 100 subseries cars. All Shimonoseki-based cars were also of the 100 subseries. In the November 1982 timetable revision, six cars (101, 102, 113–116) were transferred from Mukainomachi to Akita, and the "Dewa", the successor train that took over the express baggage transport to the Niigata area previously handled by the old "Chokai", as well as the "Akebono" Nos. 1 and 6, which were increased by upgrading one round trip of the "Tsugaru", which had similarly handled baggage transport north of Yamagata Station, were limited to 100 subseries assignments. Later, Shimonoseki-based cars moved to Miyahara with the appearance of the Suha 25, and Shinagawa-based cars progressively moved to Oku and Aomori following the abolition of the "Asakaze" and changes in assignments. In 1990, after the JR privatization, two cars were rebuilt as the 500 subseries, of which No. 510 was further rebuilt as the Kaya 27.
No. 102 has exposed rain gutters and was given gold bands. No. 112, like 510, was made non-through-type, with black rubber, and gold-banded.
As of April 2015 (Heisei 27), four cars (102, 109, 112, 116) were based at Aomori, but all were scrapped by November of that year. They had previously been used on trains such as the "Akebono" and "Nihonkai". Some Miyahara-based cars were also used on the "Twilight Express".

=== Yume Kukan ===
To explore the direction of next-generation sleeper rolling stock, JR East manufactured three cars in 1989 (Heisei 1) and displayed them as "buildings shaped like railway cars" at its own exhibition booth "Yume Kukan '89" (in the plaza in front of Sakuragicho Station) at the Yokohama Exposition held that year. After a similar display in front of Kaihin-Makuhari Station, they were used as actual railway rolling stock on group private trains and extra trains, beginning with those of the "Hokutosei" system.
Because they have no power generation equipment of their own, the Yume Kukan cannot operate as a formation on its own and is coupled with 24 series or 14 series passenger cars that have power generation equipment. For this reason, the basic structure of the car body, running equipment such as bogies and brakes, and specifications such as service power are all aligned with the 24 series passenger cars, and the type is also part of the 24 series. Accordingly, the Yume Kukan cars are the first and last 24 series passenger cars newly built after the establishment of JR.
From December 30, 1992 (Heisei 4) to New Year's Day of the following year, they also entered Kyushu on the group train "Meguri Ai Express", operated as part of a TBS television special program. On that occasion, the formation was made up of three cars from the 14 series "Super Express Rainbow" plus one 14 series sleeper car and one 14 series seating car.
Drawing on the design philosophy of the "Orient Express '88", which visited Japan the previous year, 1988 (Showa 63), the interiors and exterior paint schemes incorporate designs unique to each car. The design approach of this type was carried over to the development of the E26 series passenger cars, the private-room sleeper cars later put into service as the "Cassiopeia".
They have quite luxurious and ample equipment, which even included facilities rare on trains, such as televisions and baths.

OROne 25 901 "Deluxe Sleeper"
A class A sleeper with one two-person private room, the "Excellent Suite", and two "Superior Twin" rooms, all equipped with bathrooms. Capacity is six. Manufactured by Nippon Sharyo, with interiors by Takashimaya. The paint scheme is blue on the upper half, silver on the lower half and around the side windows, with gold stripes. Because this car is equipped with 14/24 series power conversion equipment, it must be coupled whenever power is supplied from a 14 series car.

OhaFu 25 901 "Lounge Car"
A lobby car used as shared space, with a bar lounge inside, sofas, and a player piano. The conductor's room is provided at one end of the car. Manufactured by Fuji Heavy Industries, with interiors by the Matsuya department store. Incidentally, the interior nameplates were not the then-standard Fuji Heavy Industries type, but an elaborate, original design. The paint scheme is a two-tone scheme with the base color crimson and the window surrounds beige, with gold pinstripes, resembling the paint division of Orient Express Pullman cars.

Oshi 25 901 "Dining Car"
A dining car with an observation room, coupled at the rear end of the train. It also has private rooms, with a kitchen arranged at the rear of the car. Capacity is 18 in the observation section and four in the private room section. Manufactured by Tokyu Car, with interiors by Tokyu Department Store. Initially no wipers were installed on the observation room, but an additional modification later installed two wipers. The paint scheme is metallic green with gold stripes. Equipment used during pushing operation between Oku Rolling Stock Center and Ueno Station is installed in the observation room section.
Commercial operation ended in March 2008 (Heisei 20). The lounge car and dining car were scrapped on June 9, 2009 (Heisei 21), and the Deluxe Sleeper on December 16, 2011 (Heisei 23), but all three cars are preserved. (See "Preserved rolling stock in Japan" below.)

== Rebuilt cars ==
This section describes rebuilt cars within the type, as well as cars rebuilt and transferred in from other series. Many cars of this type underwent rebuilding for transfer into other series for operational reasons and the like, but for those, see the articles of the series into which they were transferred.

=== JNR era ===

Kani 25
A rebuilt power and baggage car that succeeded the role of the Maya 20, which had been active within Kyushu as the power car when 20 series passenger car formations were split and combined. In the wholesale timetable revision accompanying the opening of the Sanyo Shinkansen to Hakata on March 10, 1975, sleeper express trains between Kansai and Kyushu were extensively reorganized, but because the "Akatsuki" was short of cars due to the aforementioned halt in 14 series sleeper production, and because the two-tier class B berths of the 24 series Type 25, which had been used before the revision, were well received by users, one round trip of 24 series Type 25 operation was continued after the revision. However, because this operation involved combined running of the "Myojo/Akatsuki" between Shin-Osaka and Tosu stations, the "Akatsuki" would lose service power within the Nagasaki Main Line. Therefore, as a power car for splitting and combining operations, the Kani 22, which among 20 series power cars had low baggage loading capacity and limited use, was rebuilt at Kokura Works (now Kokura General Rolling Stock Center) in 1975 and transferred into the 24 series. In the rebuilding, ventilators were installed at the former pantograph mounting locations, which had been removed in the 20 series era, and the output voltage of the generators was changed from 600 V to 440 V by rewinding the coils.
Both cars were allocated to the Nagasaki Passenger and Freight Car District (now Nagasaki Rolling Stock Center of the Nagasaki Railway Business Department), but with the wholesale timetable revision of October 2, 1978 (Showa 53), the combined running of the two trains was dissolved, and at the same time the "Akatsuki" was replaced by the newly built 14 series Type 15, which like the 24 series Type 25 had two-tier class B berths; one car was scrapped that year. The remaining car was transferred to the Mukainomachi Depot as a spare for the Kani 24 and Kaya 24, and after being used on the "Suisei" and "Myojo", it was scrapped in 1984 (Showa 59), and the type ceased to exist.
Kani 22 53, 2 → 1, 2

Oshi 24, 100 subseries
A dining car rebuilt from the Oshi 14 in 1975 (Showa 50). When the 24 series were diverted to trains serving Tokyo, the Oshi 24 cars were insufficient, but rather than expanding the 0 subseries to curb new-build costs, the shortfall was covered by rebuilding from surplus 14 series dining cars, the Oshi 14. Five cars were rebuilt. When the sleeper cars were replaced by the 24 series Type 25 in 1976 (Showa 51), they were retained with their white bands unchanged; as with the 0 subseries, they gained silver tape bands around the time the Oha 24 700 subseries appeared. After the privatization and division of JNR, all five cars were inherited by JR Kyushu and used on the "Hayabusa" and "Fuji". In 1999 (Heisei 11), dining cars were removed from the "Hayabusa" and "Fuji", so they were scrapped. Card-type public telephones were installed after the privatization, but because dining cars were removed in 1997 (Heisei 9), they were relocated to the lounge car.
Oshi 14 5, 6, 10, 11, 14 → 101–105

OROne 24, 100 subseries
Class A sleepers rebuilt from the OROne 14 in 1982 and 1986. Open-room type. There were no major changes in appearance or interior. Car 101 was inherited by JR East, and 102 and 103 by JR West, but 101 was further rebuilt as SuroNe 24 552, and with the abolition of the "Ginga", the remaining two cars were also all scrapped by 2009.
OROne 14 11, 9, 10 → 101–103

Oha 24, 700 subseries
JNR's first lounge car, created by utilizing surplus cars to revitalize sleeper express trains whose utilization rates had been declining. Between 1985 and 1986, all cars were rebuilt from the Oshi 14 and OhaNe 14 at Omiya Works.
The window arrangement differs depending on the donor car, such as the presence or absence of a business-use door. The paint scheme was changed from white bands to silver bands, with four bands between the upper and lower bands, placed on the left and right near the center of the car body. The interior is equipped with sofas, rotating chairs, and a bar counter.
They were coupled to the "Hayabusa" in 1985 and the "Fuji" in 1986. Because the coupling of this car increased the tonnage rating, the electric locomotives for DC electrified sections were changed from the preceding JNR Class EF65 1000 subseries to the JNR Class EF66, formerly used for hauling high-speed freight trains.
A card-type public telephone was installed in 1997, but relocated to the OROne 15 in 2005.
They were initially allocated to the Shinagawa Passenger Car District, but were later transferred to the Kumamoto Passenger and Freight Car District (now Kumamoto Rolling Stock Center of the Kumamoto Railway Business Department), and all cars were inherited by JR Kyushu. They were used on the "Fuji" and "Hayabusa" for a long time, but in 2005, with the conversion of these trains to the 14 series, they left regular operation and were scrapped within the year.
Oshi 14 9, 4; OhaNe 14 2, 4, 67 → Oha 24 701–705

OhaNe 24, 700 subseries
A four-person class B private berth "Quartet" car that appeared in March 1986 for the "Fuji". Rebuilt at Omiya Works and Ofuna Works.
As with the OhaNe 14 700 subseries rebuilt for the "Sakura" and "Mizuho", partition walls were installed in the interior to create four-person private rooms. With the rebuilding, the paint scheme was changed from white bands to silver bands.
In November 1986, with the transfer of jurisdiction over the "Fuji" passenger cars' home depot and the introduction of common operation with the "Hayabusa", audio equipment was installed and gold banding was applied; thereafter they were coupled to the upgraded "Asakaze Nos. 1 and 4". Allocated to the Shinagawa Passenger Car District and inherited by JR East, they lost their purpose when the "Asakaze Nos. 1 and 4" were abolished in 1994. They were subsequently used on extra trains coupled with the Yume Kukan, but all cars were scrapped in 2000.
14, 62, 34 → 701–703

SuhaNe 25, 700 subseries
Introduced in 1987 for the "Asakaze Nos. 1 and 4" as JNR's first two-person class B private berth "Duet" car, through rebuilding of the OhaNe 25 100 subseries. The rebuilding was carried out by Omiya Works, Takatori Works, and Hatabu Works.
It has eight two-person class B private rooms, with the rooms alternately allocated between the first and second floors.
The car ends are equipped with a shower room, also a first for JNR, a mini lobby with L-shaped sofas and a round table, and a beverage vending machine corner. There is also a machine room with a water tank for the shower room.
It was accepted as a pioneering car for its time, and can be said to have led the way in the compartmentalization of later sleeper trains such as the "Hokutosei" and "Twilight Express".
Inherited by JR East, it left all operation with the abolition of the "Asakaze Nos. 1 and 4" in 1994. Like the OhaNe 24-700, it was subsequently used on extra trains coupled with the Yume Kukan, and all cars were scrapped in 2000.
OhaNe 25 219, 222, 223 → SuhaNe 25 701–703

OROne 25, 700 subseries
A grade-up rebuilt car of the OROne 25 0 subseries that appeared between 1986 and 1987 for the "Asakaze Nos. 1 and 4". All rebuilding was handled by Takatori Works.
Cosmetic seats were installed in the private rooms, and the interiors were renewed with improvements to the berth lighting, installation of audio equipment, replacement of the washstand table, changing the floor coverings of the entrance platform and toilet corridor to cigarette-resistant material, and changing the interior color of the toilets. A feedthrough line with the Oshi 24 700 subseries was also added.
Externally, the scheme was changed from two silver stainless bands to three gold bands, but there was almost no change in capacity or other equipment.
With the abolition of the "Asakaze Nos. 1 and 4" in 1994, they were diverted to the "Hakutsuru", which had been converted to passenger cars from 583 series EMUs that year. At that time, the upper band was painted starting above the emergency exit, and the moquette was also refurbished.
The "Hakutsuru" was also abolished in 2002 (Heisei 14), so all cars were scrapped the following year.
8, 11, 12 → 701–703

Oshi 24, 700 subseries
A dining car that appeared in 1987 with the grade-up rebuilding of the "Asakaze Nos. 1 and 4". The rebuilding was carried out at Omiya Works (701) and Takatori Works (702–705).
Cars 701–703 have blue-toned interiors evoking a starry sky. Lounge-style sofas were installed at the car ends.
Cars 704 and 705 have red, white, and wood-grain interiors evoking the Orient. They were also prototypes for direct sleeper trains to Hokkaido, and the design concept of these cars was carried over to the dining cars of the "Hokutosei" and "Twilight Express".
They were used on the "Asakaze Nos. 1 and 4" and the "Izumo Nos. 1 and 4" (→ "Izumo"), and were subsequently also used as onboard sales bases and substitutes for lounge cars even after the abolition of dining car service, but became reserve cars with the abolition of the "Izumo" in 2006.
1–5 → 701–705

Rebuilds of the OhaNe 25 and OhaNefu 25 for the "Asakaze Nos. 1 and 4"
Rebuilding was also applied to the ordinary class B sleeper cars for the grade-up of the "Asakaze Nos. 1 and 4".
Carpets were laid on the corridors and floors to reduce noise when walking, and the interiors were renewed, including changing the bed moquette from the previous blue to orange.
As with the other rebuilt cars, the paint scheme bands were changed to gold, and one more band was added under the roof in addition to the conventional position.
After inheritance by JR East, they were also coupled to the "Izumo" in common operation. With the abolition of the "Asakaze Nos. 1 and 4" in 1994 (Heisei 6), some were diverted to the "Hakutsuru", and were subsequently also used on the "Akebono" and "Nihonkai".

OROne 25, 500 subseries
A two-person class A private room "Twin Deluxe (DX)" sleeper that appeared through rebuilding of the OhaNe 25 between 1987, in the final years of JNR, and 1988, after the privatization of JNR, in connection with the plan for direct sleeper trains to Hokkaido (later the "Hokutosei") ahead of the opening of the Seikan Tunnel. The rebuilding was carried out at Tsuchizaki Works (501, 504, 505) and Omiya Works (502, 503, 506).
The private rooms are equipped with two-tier berths, a sofa, a table, and a monitor, but no washroom. After the privatization of JNR, the cars rebuilt at JR East received minor changes such as the addition of a magnetic card lock function to the private room doors.
The provision of small windows at the top left of each window on the berth side for the two-tier berths is a distinguishing external feature. The height of the windows on the berth side differs depending on the donor car before rebuilding (the OhaNe 25 0 and 100 subseries).
The passenger doors were also made sliding type, and the heating equipment was strengthened.
As for the paint scheme, the two silver bands were changed to three gold bands. Note that the topmost gold band on the berth side is interrupted in eight places to avoid the small windows.
Five cars were rebuilt in the JNR era, of which three were inherited by JR Hokkaido and two by JR East, and one car was additionally rebuilt at JR East in fiscal 1987. In addition, for the one year from their appearance until the opening of the Seikan Tunnel, they were provisionally incorporated into the "Yuzuru", and the JR Hokkaido cars were also operated in the form of a loan to JR East. After the opening of the Seikan Tunnel, they were placed on the "Hokutosei".
With the reduction in the frequency of the "Hokutosei" in the March 15, 2008 timetable revision, the JR Hokkaido cars (three, 501–503) were scrapped that year and transferred to Myanmar Railways. Cars 504–506, based at Oku Rolling Stock Center of JR East: 505 was scrapped in September 2015, and the remaining 504 and 506 were scrapped on April 8, 2016, eliminating the subseries.
OhaNe 25 237, 14, 19, 233, 236, 235 → OROne 25 501–506

Sushi 24, 500 subseries
As with the aforementioned OROne 25 500 subseries, a dining car introduced between 1987, in the final years of JNR, and 1989, after the privatization of JNR, in preparation for the plan for a direct sleeper train to Hokkaido (later the "Hokutosei") at the time of the opening of the Seikan Tunnel.
The rebuilding was carried out at Matto Works (501), Suita Works (502), Niitsu Works (503–507), and Naebo Works (508).
Because sufficient numbers of the Oshi 24, the 24 series dining car, were unavailable, the shortfall was met by rebuilding the Sashi 481 and Sashi 489, the dining cars of the 485 and 489 series EMUs, which had become surplus with the elimination of all dining cars from limited express EMUs. The donor cars selected for rebuilding were young cars built in 1973–1974, equipped with AU13E air conditioning units.
Because they were rebuilt from limited express EMUs, their exterior differs greatly from the other 24 series passenger cars, including differences in the body cross-section and the direct reuse of the air conditioning units and bogies from the donor cars, making them conspicuous within a formation.
As with the aforementioned Oshi 24 704 and 705, the interiors are in the European passenger car style, but the table arrangement is a spacious one, with two-seat and four-seat tables on either side. All the simplified driving equipment on the donor cars was removed, and the driver's windows on the end faces were filled in.
Three cars (501–503) were introduced in the JNR era and inherited by JR Hokkaido after the privatization. At completion, as with the Oshi 24 701–703, they had four-seat tables and sofas on both sides, were formed into a five-car train flanked by two Suhafu 14, 14 series seating cars, and were used on group and event trains. This interior was changed before the "Hokutosei" began operation, and the cars were given the nickname "Gran Chariot".
After the privatization, four cars (504–507) were added at JR East and one car (508) at JR Hokkaido.
The paint scheme consists of three gold bands on blue. However, No. 508 alone has a four-band scheme with two bands in the middle, following the Alpha Continental Express, with vertical bands at the car ends and beside the doors (hereinafter called the "Alcon band"), and the position and thickness of the bands also differ from the other cars. The four JR Hokkaido cars (501–503, 508) were fitted with a dedicated emblem at the right edge of each side of the body with the "Hokutosei" operation.
The windows of the kitchen also differ from car to car: all replaced with fixed windows (501–503), original type with only the left one plugged (504–507), and original type (508). In addition, on the four JR East cars (504–507), the ventilation openings for the water cooler, located between the passenger windows and passage windows, are plugged.
With the reduction in the frequency of the "Hokutosei" in the March 15, 2008 timetable revision, the Hokkaido cars were scrapped that year and transferred to Myanmar Railways.
JR East's 505 was scrapped on October 20, 2015. Car 507 was also scrapped on April 8, 2016. Car 504 was scrapped on April 15, 2016, transported to "Pure Village Higashi-Kawaguchi", and operates as a restaurant.
Sashi 481-67, 75, 76, 64, 68, 50 → Sushi 24 501–505, 508
Sashi 489-83, 7 → Sushi 24 506, 507

Kani 24, 500 subseries
Cars rebuilt from the Kani 24 0 and 100 subseries with Seikan Tunnel compatibility, cold-weather, and snow-resistant modifications, for use on Seikan Blue Trains. Eleven cars were rebuilt between 1987 and 1990. The rebuilding included enhanced insulation of various equipment and the installation of snow-cutting devices on the engine air intake.
The body bands were changed from two silver to three gold, but No. 510 was completed with silver bands; subsequently, its front doors were filled in and its front made non-through-type, simultaneously given white bands, and it was later rebuilt as the Kaya 27. Rebuilds of the OhaNe 25 and OhaNefu 25 for Hokkaido
For the same reasons as the aforementioned rebuilt cars, severe cold weather modifications conforming to the Hokkaido-oriented rebuilt cars of the 14 series sleepers (500 subseries) were also carried out on the ordinary class B sleeper cars, including making the passenger doors sliding type and strengthening the heating equipment. Note that the sliding door windows use metal retainers, unlike the H-rubber retainers of the 14 series (the OROne 25 500 subseries rebuilt at the same time is similar).
In parallel with this rebuilding, as with the grade-up cars of the "Asakaze Nos. 1 and 4", the exterior was changed from two silver bands to three gold bands, and the interior equipment was renewed, but there were no changes in car numbers.
As with the aforementioned OROne 25 500 subseries, some cars were inherited by JR Hokkaido after the JR privatization, but they were incorporated into the "Yuzuru" and used until the opening of the Seikan Tunnel.
For the Nihonkai, only cold-weather, snow-resistant, and Seikan Tunnel compatibility modifications were applied. Sliding doors were not applied. Most remained with white and silver bands.

=== JR Hokkaido ===

==== "Hokutosei" rebuilt cars ====

OhaNefu 24, 500 subseries
In 1989, OhaNe 14 500 subseries cars made surplus by the conversion of the expresses "Soya" and "Tenpoku" to diesel multiple units were rebuilt to add Nos. 3 and 4 services. The bodies reuse the OhaNe 14, a conductor's room is provided between the deck and the passenger room, and the end face on the conductor's room side has windows only on the left side. The through doors were changed to hinged doors, and a train name indicator was installed. The donor cars had three-tier berths, but these were made two-tier during the rebuilding. The air conditioning was Type AU76, but was rebuilt to AU76B in 1997, and the bogies are TR217F-modified, compatible with 110 km/h. The crew room was rebuilt into a women's powder room, and women's toilets and cosmetic seats were replaced.
Because the passenger doors remain sliding type, the door windows use H-rubber retainers.
The paint scheme was also changed from two white bands to three gold bands, with bands applied even over the sliding doors. No. 502 has no JR mark.
They are normally coupled in the middle of a formation and rarely at the rear.
With the end of regular operation in the March 14, 2015 timetable revision, they lost their purpose; both cars were transferred from Sapporo Depot to Sapporo Freight Terminal Station and scrapped on April 5, 2015.
OhaNe 14 507, 508 → OhaNefu 24 501, 502

With the end of regular "Hokutosei" operation in the March 14, 2015 timetable revision, they lost their purpose; No. 2 was sent to Naebo Works for dismantling, and the remaining three cars were transferred from Sapporo Depot to Sapporo Freight Terminal Station. All were scrapped on April 5, 2015.

As with the OhaNefu 24 500 subseries, cars rebuilt in 1989 from surplus OhaNe 14 500 subseries cars to add Nos. 3 and 4 services. The air conditioning is AU76 (rebuilt to AU76B from 1998 onward), the bogies are TR217F-modified, compatible with 110 km/h, and the berths were rebuilt from three-tier to two-tier.
The doors remain the sliding type (door windows with H-rubber retainers) of the donor cars, and the paint scheme was changed from two white bands to three gold bands, with bands applied over the sliding doors as with the OhaNefu 24 500 subseries.
They were also used on the "Hamanasu", in addition to the "Hokutosei".
No. 504 was scrapped in 2008 and transferred to Myanmar Railways. The remaining 501–503 were also scrapped in March 2016.

==== Power supply cars ====

Mani 24, 500 subseries
A power supply car that appeared after rebuilding by JR East and JR Hokkaido from the Mani 50, a 50 series baggage car, in anticipation of a shortage of power cars for Seikan train operations. The bogies are the same TR230 series as in the 50 series era, but the brake equipment, which had been CL automatic brakes only, was brought in line with that of the 24 series. Because the 50 series was the donor, the car body has no waist taper, but the roof was modified to soften the sense of incongruity as a formation and to provide an opening for taking out the power engine, as with the Kani 24, bringing the roof height in line with the other cars. The rear end face is non-through type. In addition, cold-weather and snow-resistant modifications were also carried out for operation in Hokkaido, and the cars were classified as the 500 subseries. Two DMF13Z-G power engines are installed, and the baggage room load is 1 t.
No. 501 belonged to JR East and No. 502 to JR Hokkaido, but 501 was scrapped and dismantled in June 2006. No. 502 was also scrapped in March 2010, and the Mani 24 ceased to exist.
The JR East cars were also used on the "Izumo" and others, in addition to the "Hokutosei", "Elm", and the Yume Kukan.

==== Rebuilt cars for the "Asakaze Nos. 3 and 2" and "Seto" ====
All of these were rebuilt between 1989 and the beginning of 1990 with the grade-up of the "Asakaze Nos. 3 and 2" (→ "Asakaze", commonly called the "Shimonoseki Asakaze") and the "Seto". Both trains were changed from formations consisting entirely of class B sleeper cars to formations incorporating one class A private sleeper car and one lounge car each, and because they ran on DC electrified sections for their entire routes, for some formations the Kani 24 power cars were removed and pantographs were installed on the lounge cars to collect current from the overhead lines. These cars were progressively put into service from the beginning of 1990 to the March timetable revision of that year.

OhaNefu 25, 300 subseries (301–303)
Cars with a baggage room installed on the OhaNefu 25 100 subseries. They were rebuilt because, among the "Asakaze Nos. 3 and 2" and "Seto" formations, those that switched their power system to overhead line collection from the lobby car Suha 25 discontinued the coupling of the Kani 24, making it necessary to newly provide a baggage transport space within the formation. A baggage room with a load of 3 t was newly installed on the crew room side, the conventional passenger doors were changed to sliding doors for the baggage room, and the deck and passenger doors were relocated between the baggage room and the passenger room. The feedthrough lines were also rebuilt to allow changes of direction, and the cars were formed to face the same direction as the Kani 24. Because passengers could no longer go to the crew room with the new baggage room, an interphone was installed. The baggage room load was reduced compared with the Kani 24, and shelves were installed in the baggage room instead. Because the baggage room is nominally a business room, the "Ni" indicating a baggage car is not included in the type, and no type change was made. In addition, a jumper plug for controlling the lowering of the Suha 25 pantograph from the locomotive was installed, together with the OhaNefu 25 at the end of the formation.
With the abolition of the "Asakaze" in 2005, all three cars became reserve cars, but all were scrapped in 2008.

It also became necessary to be able to lower the pantograph from the locomotive side in emergencies, and pantograph lowering control devices for the Suha 25 were installed on the JNR Class EF66 electric locomotives allocated to JR West's Shimonoseki Depot (now Shimonoseki General Rolling Stock Center, Operations and Maintenance Center) and the JNR Class EF65 1000 subseries allocated to JR East's Tabata Depot and permanently stationed at Shinagawa Depot, and modification work was carried out to attach jumper plugs for wiring feedthrough on the Class EF66.

== Changes in operation ==
From the mid-1990s, after the JR privatization, the trains using the 24 series gradually declined, and after the abolition of the "Nihonkai" in 2012, regular operation was limited to the "Akebono" (mixed with the Type 25), excluding compartmentalized rebuilt cars and cars transferred in from the 14 series. With the end of regular "Akebono" operation in March 2014 (Heisei 26), and the subsequent extra "Akebono" also no longer being scheduled after January 2015, all cars left operation.
As of 2013 (Heisei 25), the 24 series Type 25 was in service on the "Hokutosei", "Twilight Express", "Akebono", and the express "Hamanasu". After the end of regular "Akebono" operation in March 2014 (Heisei 26), the "Akebono" ended operation after the December 2014–January 2015 extra trains. In March of the same year, the "Hokutosei" (regular) and "Twilight Express" were abolished. The "Hokutosei" subsequently became an extra train, but extra operation also ended with the up train departing Sapporo on August 22, 2015 (Heisei 27). The "Twilight Express", meanwhile, was operated as the "Special Twilight Express", mainly as a tour group extra train between Kyoto and Osaka stations and Shimonoseki Station, but ended operation with the departure from Shimonoseki on March 21, 2016. On the express "Hamanasu", which remained as the last regular operation, OhaNe 25 and OhaNefu 25 cars rebuilt for mixed operation with the 14 series were used (the OhaNe 24 500 subseries, cars rebuilt from the OhaNe 14, were also used in common), but the "Hamanasu" ended operation with the train arriving at Sapporo Station on March 22, 2016 (Heisei 28), and all left operation.

== Current status ==

=== Current rolling stock ===
At the time of the privatization and division of JNR in 1987, a total of 544 cars were inherited: 29 by Hokkaido Railway Company (JR Hokkaido), 241 by East Japan Railway Company (JR East), 155 by West Japan Railway Company (JR West), and 119 by Kyushu Railway Company (JR Kyushu) (all JNR-era scrapping was due to accidents, involving two cars: OhaNefu 25 18 and OhaNefu 25 104 in the Nishi-Akashi Station train derailment accident). However, scrapping progressed due to the abolition of sleeper trains and the aging of rolling stock, and all JR Hokkaido, JR Kyushu, and JR West cars were scrapped. As of April 1, 2026 (Reiwa 8), one car belongs to JR East. The breakdown is as follows.

==== Hokkaido Railway Company (JR Hokkaido) ====

Sapporo Depot
Twenty-six cars were in service as of April 2015 (Heisei 27), but all were scrapped within fiscal 2015 (fiscal Heisei 27). They had been used on the "Hokutosei" and "Hamanasu", but 19 passenger cars for Hokutosei use (two OhaNefu 24, five OhaNefu 25, three SuhaNe 25, eight OhaNe 25, and one Kani 24) were scrapped on April 5, 2015 (Heisei 27) with the end of their operation, and 16 of these were sent for scrapping hauled by JR Freight Class DF200 diesel locomotives.
In May 2015 (Heisei 27) they were stored on a freight siding at Muroran Port, but on September 14, dismantling of the 19 cars began at Jinyamachi Station in Muroran City, Hokkaido.
While dismantling progressed, there was a movement to preserve cars in Hokuto City, led by the chamber of commerce; on March 28, 2016, after a press conference, a crowdfunding campaign was launched for the preservation of OhaNefu 25 2. The first target of 10 million yen was reached on April 17 of the same year, and the following day, April 18, the second target, 12.5 million yen for the transport costs for preserving SuhaNe 25 501, was also reached. Regarding the preservation of these two cars, the travel company "Core Agency Niseko" in Kutchan Town, Hokkaido, had also been considering a movement to preserve cars using its own funds for the purpose of tourism resources in the Niseko area, and announced its consideration of preservation on September 16, 2015 (Heisei 27), but with the aforementioned transfer to Hokuto City confirmed, and because there were no longer any cars available for transfer within JR Hokkaido, it withdrew its plan, including its locomotives.

== Facilities using sleeper equipment ==
Using "Hokutosei" class B berths and private-room berths (used car number plates: "OhaNe 25 238", "OROne 25 506", "Sushi 24 507", "ORohaNe 24 554", "OROne 25 504")
"Train Hostel Hokutosei" (Chuo Ward, Tokyo): To meet the diverse accommodation needs of foreign visitors to Japan, JR East newly built accommodation facilities using Hokutosei class B berths and private-room berths in an existing building, and opened for business on December 15, 2016. Targeting inbound tourists and railway fans, it was promoted as "reasonably priced from the low 2,000 yen range, with the atmosphere of a night train"; operation was handled by R.project, development by JR East Urban Development, and design by OpenA. A shared kitchen using the seats and tables of the "Gran Chariot", the former "Hokutosei" dining car, was also installed. The private rooms used class A sleeper Royal berths. Most of the open-plan berths used class B berths, but some spaces also reused class A sleeper Twin DX berths. Operation by R.project ended at the end of July 2021 (Reiwa 3), and the business closed.

== Transfers abroad ==

=== State Railway of Thailand ===
Of the two JR Kyushu OhaNe 25 cars, one was transferred to the State Railway of Thailand in 1998 and one in 2005.
In 2008, a total of 28 scrapped 24 series sleepers were transferred from JR West to the State Railway of Thailand. This is the largest number of sleeper passenger cars held from transfers from Japan. Because Thai railways are meter gauge, the bogies were rebuilt, and modifications were carried out including the addition of steps to suit low platforms, toilet modifications to suit the State Railway of Thailand's waste handling circumstances and Thai excretion habits (removal of waste tanks and installation of Thai-style toilet showers), and color changes (initially, the end faces were changed to warning colors; the sides had the same colors as in the Japanese era). In addition, because the 24 series had underfloor generators, they could be used on a per-car basis. Because their overall length and width exceeded the conventional loading gauge of the State Railway of Thailand, the operating sections were initially limited, but the loading gauge was permitted with the start of operation on the Northern Line described below.
Initially, the 14 series seating and sleeper cars were introduced as the "JR Class" on the Southern Line express Trains Nos. 85 and 86 between Bangkok and Trang, and the 24 series on the sleeper express Trains Nos. 1 and 2 connecting Bangkok and Chiang Mai on the Northern Line. However, some of the former were scrapped in the Hua Hin derailment accident of October 2009, and both the 14 and 24 series have since been removed from Southern Line operations.
The latter Northern Line express Trains Nos. 1 and 2 were given the nickname "Nakhonpin" and were the State Railway of Thailand's flagship trains, targeting foreign tourists and the wealthy. However, subsequently the cars used on these trains were replaced by ANS40 passenger cars made by Korea's Daewoo Heavy Industries, so they were diverted to Trains Nos. 13 and 14 on the same section. From around 2012, the 14 and 24 series passenger cars underwent body maintenance work involving the replacement of air conditioning, and the formations of these trains became a mix of conventional sleeper passenger cars with 14 and 24 series cars. In 2016, new sleeper passenger cars made by China's CRRC were delivered to the State Railway of Thailand and put into operation, and under this influence the 14 and 24 series passenger cars left regular operation on Trains Nos. 13 and 14 in November of that year. By this time, the 14 and 24 series had been changed to a purple two-tone State Railway of Thailand livery.
In addition, from 2009 some of Trains Nos. 67 and 68, running between Bangkok and Ubon Ratchathani on the southern route of the Northeastern Line, also included 14 and 24 series sleeper cars, but from around March 2013 the 14 and 24 series were removed from operation.
After losing regular operation on Trains Nos. 13 and 14 in 2016, they were mainly assigned to extra trains. During this period the 14 and 24 series underwent further refurbishment work and were repainted in a red-and-white two-tone scheme similar to the new CRRC passenger cars.
After the COVID-19 pandemic, in July 2024, the Laotian section of the northern route of the State Railway of Thailand's Northeastern Line was extended from Thanaleng station to Vientiane (Khamsavath) station. As the sleeper passenger cars and air-conditioned seating cars of Trains Nos. 133 and 134, the international trains connecting Bangkok and Vientiane that began operation with this, the 14 and 24 series sleepers and 14 series seating cars were selected, and regular operation of the 14 and 24 series resumed. Among used railway vehicles transferred abroad from Japan after the war, the 14 and 24 series cars coupled to these trains are thought to be the first to operate across national borders as regular international passenger trains.

=== Malayan Railway ===
In November 2010, one car was transferred from JR West to the Malayan Railway Administration (KTM), and from November 15 to 16 of the same year it was transported by land to Shimonoseki Port together with seven 14 series seating cars. From December 16, 2011, it began operating on KTM Intercity as the "Malayan Tiger Train" (meaning "Tiger of Malaya") between JB Sentral and Tumpat stations, but operations are currently suspended and it is stored within Gumas station.

=== Myanmar Railways ===
JR Hokkaido cars treated as scrapped on April 30, 2008 have been transferred to Myanmar Railways.
